description: Mandatory label information, reading nutritional labelling and Reference Intakes, and how marketing shapes food choices.
content_html:
Reading the Label — and Resisting the Marketing

Every pre-packed food product in the UK must carry specific information required by law. Alongside this mandatory information, manufacturers add optional content designed to make their product look as appealing — and as healthy — as possible. Knowing the difference between what is legally required and what is promotional is a critical consumer skill. On top of that, marketing techniques — from buy-one-get-one-free offers to celebrity endorsements on social media — can quietly steer purchases away from the foods that best meet a person's nutritional needs.

Mandatory Information on Pre-Packed Food

UK food labelling legislation, aligned with the principles established by both EU regulations and the Food Standards Agency (FSA), requires the following information on all pre-packed food:

  • Name of the food — the legal name, not just a brand name. A product called “Sunny Gold” must also state “orange-flavoured drink” if it contains little actual juice.
  • List of ingredients — in descending order of weight. If sugar is the first ingredient listed, it is the predominant ingredient by weight.
  • Allergen information — the 14 major allergens (including nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, fish and shellfish) must be emphasised in the ingredients list, typically in bold text.
  • Net quantity — the weight or volume of the product.
  • Date marking — either a “use by” date (safety — do not consume after this date) or a “best before” date (quality — still safe to eat after this date but quality may have declined).
  • Storage conditions and instructions for use — e.g. “keep refrigerated below 5°C” or “once opened, consume within two days”.
  • Name and address of the manufacturer, packer or seller within the UK or EU.
  • Country of origin — required for specific foods such as beef, lamb, pork, chicken, fish and honey.
  • Nutrition declaration — mandatory for most pre-packed foods. Must include energy (kJ and kcal), fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt per 100 g or 100 ml.
Key Fact

“Use by” = safety. Do not eat the food after this date even if it looks and smells fine — it may contain dangerous levels of bacteria. “Best before” = quality. The food is safe to eat after this date but may have declined in flavour or texture. This distinction often appears as a 1-mark identification question.

Non-Mandatory Information

Manufacturers may choose to include additional information that goes beyond legal requirements. Common examples include: provenance information (“made in Yorkshire”, “free-range eggs from Cornish hens”); serving suggestions (“serve with fresh salad”); quality claims (“award-winning recipe”); and environmental or welfare certifications such as the Fairtrade mark or the RSPCA Assured logo. These claims are voluntary but must not be misleading.

How to Interpret Nutritional Labelling

The mandatory nutrition declaration shows values per 100 g (or 100 ml for drinks). Manufacturers often also show values per portion, though the declared portion size may be smaller than what a typical person actually eats. A bag of crisps labelled “per serving (25 g)” may contain two servings; a person who eats the whole bag consumes double the labelled figures.

Reference Intakes (RIs) are the guideline daily amounts for an average adult consuming 2,000 kcal per day. The label may show the percentage of the RI that a serving contributes. For example, a meal containing 3 g of salt provides 50% of the adult daily RI for salt (6 g). This helps consumers compare products at a glance.

Traffic light labelling uses colour-coded icons (red, amber or green) for fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt to make nutritional information instantly accessible. Red means high, amber means medium, green means low. A product with mostly green lights is considered a healthier choice than one with multiple red lights. Traffic light labelling is voluntary but widely used by major UK supermarkets and manufacturers.

Always compare products using per 100 g figures, not per portion, because declared portion sizes vary between brands and may not reflect real servings. To check whether a product is high, medium or low in a nutrient, use these per 100 g thresholds (aligned to FSA and traffic-light guidance): Fat: high ≥17.5 g, low ≤3 g. Saturates: high ≥5 g, low ≤1.5 g. Sugars: high ≥22.5 g, low ≤5 g. Salt: high ≥1.5 g, low ≤0.3 g. A product with 20 g sugar per 100 g is “medium” (amber) for sugars; a product with 25 g sugar per 100 g is “high” (red).

How Marketing Influences Food Choice

Food marketing is highly sophisticated. Techniques range from in-store promotions to digital advertising targeting specific demographics. The key marketing methods from the specification are:

  • Buy one get one free (BOGOF) and special offers: These promotions encourage buying larger quantities than needed, often for foods that are high in fat, sugar or salt. A household may buy three multi-packs of biscuits because of a deal, consuming more biscuits that week than they otherwise would.
  • Meal deals: A fixed-price meal deal at a supermarket or convenience store (sandwich, snack, drink) often guides the consumer toward specific products — frequently those with higher profit margins for the retailer. The drink in a meal deal is rarely water; it is usually a sugary juice or fizzy drink.
  • Media and advertising: Television, social media influencers, celebrity endorsements and sponsored content shape brand perception and product desirability. Children are particularly susceptible to advertising, which is why restrictions on junk food advertising before 9 pm exist in UK broadcast regulations.
  • Point of sale marketing: Products placed at eye level, near tills or at the end of supermarket aisles (called “end-of-aisle” or “gondola end” displays) sell in greater quantities than items shelved elsewhere, regardless of their nutritional quality. Sweets and chocolates placed at checkout height for children are a deliberate point-of-sale strategy.
Key Fact

Marketing shapes food choice without changing the food itself. Point-of-sale placement (near tills, end-of-aisle), promotional pricing (BOGOF, meal deals), and media advertising (social influencers, TV) all increase sales of specific products. A consumer aware of these techniques can make more deliberate, informed choices rather than impulse purchases.

Terms like “light”, “reduced fat”, “no added sugar” and “high in protein” are regulated in the UK. “Reduced fat” means at least 30% less fat than the standard version; it does not mean the product is low in fat. “No added sugar” means no sugar has been added during production but the product may still contain naturally occurring sugars (e.g. fruit sugars or lactose) that contribute significantly to total sugar intake. “Light” must mean either at least 30% fewer calories or 30% less fat than the reference product. Students must read the full nutrition declaration, not just the front-of-pack claim, to assess whether a product genuinely suits their nutritional goals.
exam_tip_html: A common error on food labelling questions is confusing “use by” with “best before”. Remember: “use by” is a safety instruction (do not eat after this date); “best before” is a quality guide (safe but quality declines). On a 9-mark Analyse question about how labelling and marketing influence food choice, separate the two issues clearly. Analyse labelling (how mandatory information helps consumers make informed decisions; how traffic-light labelling simplifies comparison) separately from marketing (how BOGOF, meal deals and point-of-sale placement bypass rational decision-making). Examine the relationship between them: a product with multiple red traffic lights but a compelling BOGOF offer may still sell strongly, which shows that marketing often overrides labelling in practice. That relationship is what earns top-band marks for analysis.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mandatory label information includes the ingredients list (in descending weight order), allergen emphasis, date marks (use by = safety; best before = quality), and the nutrition declaration per 100 g.
  • Reference Intakes (RIs) are guideline daily amounts for an average 2,000 kcal adult; traffic-light labelling colour-codes fat, saturates, sugars and salt as red, amber or green per 100 g.
  • Marketing techniques — BOGOF offers, meal deals, point-of-sale placement and media advertising — can steer consumers toward less nutritious products regardless of what the label shows.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following must be included on a pre-packed food label by law?
A) Serving suggestions
B) Country of origin for all ingredients
C) The net quantity (weight or volume) of the food
D) A photograph of the dish
State what the term 'Reference Intake (RI)' means on a food label.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the guideline daily amount for a specific nutrient or energy; 1 mark for: based on an average adult consuming 2,000 kcal per day. Accept equivalent wording.

practice_questions.text: Describe how traffic-light labelling helps a consumer compare two breakfast cereals in a supermarket.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: traffic-light labelling uses colour-coded icons (red, amber, green) for fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt (1); red indicates a high amount per 100 g, green indicates a low amount (1); the consumer can quickly see which cereal has fewer red or amber ratings and therefore which is a lower-fat or lower-sugar choice without having to interpret numerical values (1).

practice_questions.text: A supermarket places a multi-pack of sugary cereal bars at child eye-height near the checkout, reduces the price by 50% and labels the shelf 'special offer'. Explain two ways in which this marketing strategy could influence the food choices of families shopping with children.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per strategy (2 required). Strategy 1: point-of-sale placement at child eye-height near the checkout deliberately targets children who are waiting and more likely to ask for impulse purchases (1); because children see the product repeatedly at a familiar location, this means parents experience pester power and may buy foods they would otherwise have passed by (1). Strategy 2: the 50% price reduction makes the product appear highly cost-effective (1); because families on a budget are sensitive to price, the reduced cost overrides the nutritional consideration and they may buy a larger quantity than they need, consuming more sugary product over the following week (1).

practice_questions.text: A secondary school is reviewing the nutritional information on the meals it serves in its canteen. The canteen manager wants to introduce traffic-light labelling on every dish. Explain the benefits and limitations of using traffic-light labelling to help students make healthier food choices at lunchtime.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): explains clearly how traffic lights work (colour-coding fat, saturates, sugars and salt using per 100 g thresholds) and why this benefits students (quick visual scan without numerical literacy; helps identify lower-fat or lower-sugar options at a glance; raises awareness of less obvious nutrients such as salt). Then explains at least two limitations: students may select green-labelled items that don't meet their total energy needs (a green-labelled salad may not be enough for an active teenager); traffic lights reflect per 100 g figures not per portion, so a small high-sugar item may show as amber when the portion eaten is large; marketing and peer pressure may override label information; students may not understand the system. Two or three well-developed chains of reasoning.

Secure (3–4): explains benefits and at least one limitation with some development and application to the school context.

Developing (1–2): states benefits or limitations with minimal development; limited application to the scenario.

Emerging (0): superficial response with no developed reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how food marketing strategies such as buy one get one free offers, meal deals and media advertising can influence food choice, and consider whether food labelling provides an effective counterbalance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): breaks marketing into distinct components and examines how each works: BOGOF — drives bulk purchases of specific products (often high in fat/sugar/salt), meaning consumers spend more than planned and may overconsume the promoted food; the financial saving feels rational but the nutritional outcome may be negative (2). Meal deals — structure the choice away from open selection toward a fixed combination; the drink component is frequently a sugary drink, meaning consumers accept a less healthy drink because it is included in a perceived value package (2). Media and advertising — repetition creates brand preference and desire independent of nutritional merit; children particularly vulnerable (1). Analyses whether labelling counterbalances: traffic-light labelling can inform aware consumers but is voluntary; mandatory nutrition declaration provides information but requires numerical literacy; marketing operates on emotion and habit rather than information, meaning labelling may fail to counteract impulse purchasing; some consumers actively use labels, especially post-health scare or diagnosis. Examines the interaction between marketing and labelling: a product with red traffic lights but a compelling BOGOF offer may still sell strongly, demonstrating that marketing often overrides information. Sustained analysis throughout with accurate terminology.

Secure (5–7): analyses at least two marketing strategies with reasonable development; some analysis of labelling as counterbalance; mostly accurate.

Developing (2–4): describes marketing strategies with limited analysis; limited engagement with labelling.

Emerging (1): brief and mainly descriptive.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following date marks means the food must not be consumed after the date shown, for safety reasons?
On a pre-packed food label, ingredients are listed in which order?
options: Order in which they are added during cooking

knowledge_checks.q: The guideline daily amounts for energy, fat, saturates, sugars and salt for an average adult eating 2,000 kcal per day are called _____ Intakes.
On a traffic-light label, a _____ colour means the nutrient content of that component is high per 100 g.
Match each marketing technique to its description.
right: Products placed near tills or at eye level to encourage impulse purchases
A fixed-price bundle that guides consumers toward specific products
Buy one, get one free — encourages bulk buying of a promoted product

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'use by' mean on a food label?
flashcard_questions.a: A safety date — do not eat the food after this date, even if it looks fine.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'best before' mean on a food label?
flashcard_questions.a: A quality date — food is safe after this date but flavour or texture may decline.

flashcard_questions.q: In what order are ingredients listed on a food label?
flashcard_questions.a: Descending order of weight; the heaviest ingredient is listed first.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a Reference Intake (RI) on a food label?
flashcard_questions.a: The guideline daily amount for an average adult consuming 2,000 kcal per day.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a red traffic-light colour indicate on a nutrition label?
flashcard_questions.a: The product is high in that nutrient per 100 g.
Fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt — shown as red, amber or green per 100 g.
Placing products near tills or at eye level to trigger impulse purchases.
Buy one get one free — encourages bulk purchasing of a promoted product.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two pieces of mandatory information that must appear on a pre-packed food label.
flashcard_questions.a: Ingredients list and allergen emphasis (accept any two valid mandatory items).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Food Standards Agency (FSA)?
flashcard_questions.a: The UK government body responsible for food safety, food standards, and labelling guidance across the country.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should you compare nutrition labels using per 100 g figures rather than per portion?
flashcard_questions.a: Declared portion sizes vary between brands and may be smaller than a typical serving.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'reduced fat' mean on a food label in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: At least 30% less fat than the standard version of the same product.

glossary_terms.definition: The UK government body responsible for food safety and standards, including the guidance on food labelling and allergen declaration.
The guideline daily amounts for energy, fat, saturates, sugars and salt for an average adult consuming 2,000 kcal per day, used as a benchmark on food labels.
A voluntary front-of-pack system using red, amber or green colour-coded icons for fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt to show at a glance whether a food is high, medium or low in those nutrients.
